title: IB English A: Literature
description: Read across voices and perspectives. Build interpretations that are worth arguing for.

items.title: Voice and perspective
items.summary: How does a narrator shape what we know—and what we question?
items.body:
## Our guiding question
How does a narrator shape what we know—and what we question?

## Read and notice
Bring a passage or image from your current class text. Make three observations about the choices its creator has made.

## Discuss
- Which detail most strongly shapes your response?
- How might another reader interpret it differently?
- What evidence helps you explain your reading?

## Make your thinking visible
Try the close reading lab, then use the paragraph workshop to turn one interpretation into a developed response.

items.title: Paper 1
items.summary: Develop a close literary analysis of a previously unseen passage.

items.body:
## Briefing

Develop an interpretation of an unseen literary text through close analysis of its choices. Let the guiding question give the response a manageable focus. Begin with the literal situation, then explore implications, tensions, and subtleties.

The companion uses Christina Rossetti’s **“Up-Hill”** throughout. Read the complete poem there, then follow the same details through Method, Avoid, Criteria and Models. The question and commentary are teaching examples, not an official IB paper.

## Method

[Unpack the guiding question](/resources/unpacking-questions#paper-1) before selecting your evidence.


[Writing an introduction: step-by-step guidance and a worked example](/resources/paper-1-introductions?example=literature)

### Orient
Establish who speaks, what happens, and what the guiding question asks you to explore. Distinguish the speaker or narrator from the writer.

### Survey
Trace the text's movement. Notice changes in voice, tone, perspective, rhythm, setting, or argument; connect parts to the whole.

### Select
Choose precise details that develop a reading. Explain how language, form, and structure interact. A device matters because of what it does in this text.

### Construct
Form a thesis that answers the guiding question. Build paragraphs around interpretive claims, bringing several related choices together rather than touring devices.

### Verify
Test your argument against an awkward detail or a plausible alternative reading. Qualify claims the text cannot fully support. A subtle interpretation need not claim certainty about the writer’s intentions.

### Need another way in?
For poetry, try [TPCASTT](/courses/literature/resources/81a5570b-6369-4557-b98b-9d8fa1be2f52). It supports initial reading; it does not prescribe an essay structure.

The [Poetry guide](/courses/literature/text-types/8889a1cf-bfb4-4930-bc54-b693504ae80a) connects voice, line and form to a worked reading of “Up-Hill.”

[The Drama guide](/courses/literature/text-types/5131f911-d916-4135-8415-ce6ad59606ff) explains how to read dialogue, silence and stage directions, with a separate worked example from Andrew Bovell.

## Avoid

- Assuming the speaker's views are the poet's views.
- Treating symbols as having fixed meanings outside their context.
- Naming sound or structural features without explaining their effects.
- Inventing background information to resolve ambiguity.
- Forcing every detail into a reading that ignores contradictory evidence.

## Criteria

### A · Understanding and interpretation
Move from accurate literal understanding to a supported reading of implications and subtleties.

### B · Analysis and evaluation
Explain how choices create meaning, and develop why their effects matter to your interpretation.

### C · Focus and organization
Sustain a clear response to the question through connected ideas.

### D · Language
Express the reading with clarity, precision, and control.

## Practice

Try the final exchange of **“Up-Hill”** in the workspace below. Keep your first reading, use the self-check, then revise. You can export either attempt without asking for AI feedback.

For a different text, use [Passage Practice](/practice/passages) for a short unseen extract. First record a literal observation, then an inference, then the choice supporting that inference.

For a second attempt, examine a detail that complicates your first reading. Revise the claim rather than discarding inconvenient evidence.

## Field tools

- [TPCASTT poetry scaffold](/courses/literature/resources/81a5570b-6369-4557-b98b-9d8fa1be2f52)
- [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432)

Use these alongside the text. Select the prompts that help answer your question. Download the complete poem and practice question from the companion for offline work.

## Models

### A route through the whole poem
1. **Opening:** connect the uphill journey and the reply “my friend.” Difficulty is acknowledged alongside companionship.
2. **Middle:** trace the fears of finding shelter and being admitted. Explain how the answers address those specific concerns.
3. **Ending:** explore the widening from “me” to “all,” while accounting for the fatigue that remains.

This is an idea-led plan, not a requirement to write one paragraph per stanza. Each point needs precise choices and evidence.

### A worked paragraph
The companion develops the middle point into an analytical paragraph. Read it first as a continuous argument, then open the commentary to see how the claim, evidence and evaluation connect.

### A revision worth making
**Too absolute:** “The answers remove the speaker’s uncertainty.”

**More defensible:** “The answers repeatedly offer assurance, while the continuing questions preserve the speaker’s uncertainty.”

The second claim accounts for the whole exchange. It gives you more to explain, not less.

items.title: Higher Level Essay

items.body:
## Briefing

Develop a sustained argument through a focused line of inquiry into the chosen work or body of work. This page currently supports Literature HL; the core practices of inquiry, evidence selection, analysis, and revision also transfer to Language & Literature HL.

## Method

### Find an inquiry worth pursuing
Begin with a pattern, tension, or question in the text. Narrow it until you can explore particular choices in depth rather than surveying a large theme.

### Test the evidence
Collect moments that support and complicate the emerging argument. Revise the line of inquiry if it requires speculation or relies on too little textual material.

### Build and revise
Arrange paragraphs as stages in an argument. Make each analytical move serve the inquiry. After drafting, outline what each paragraph actually establishes and revise gaps or repetition.

## Avoid

- Choosing a topic so broad that the essay becomes a survey.
- Treating the line of inquiry as a label rather than an active question.
- Collecting quotations before deciding what they help establish.
- Substituting biography or secondary opinion for close analysis.
- Adding evidence without developing its implications.

## Criteria

### A · Knowledge, understanding and interpretation
Develop a supported interpretation relevant to the inquiry.

### B · Analysis and evaluation
Explain how language, style, structure, and other choices shape meaning.

### C · Focus, organization and development
Sustain and develop the inquiry through connected reasoning and integrated examples.

### D · Language
Use precise, effective language appropriate to the essay.

## Practice

Write three versions of a line of inquiry, each narrower than the previous one. For the strongest version, identify three textual moments and one possible complication.

Use the [paragraph workshop](/courses/literature/practice/4677f8b8-7908-4001-a7be-b8f450a46cfa) to test one stage of the argument.

## Field tools

Keep an inquiry log: **question · evidence · emerging claim · complication · next revision**.

Use [From observation to analysis](/courses/language-literature/resources/bfa6c8ee-0901-4cc2-b3fb-2070394d9432) to check that each paragraph explains choices rather than summarizing content.

## Models

[See how lines of inquiry develop in Lady Susan and Timon of Athens](/resources/hle-inquiries). Follow the movement from observation to choice to analytical question, then apply the process to your own studied text.


### Narrowing an inquiry
Move from a broad topic such as “power” to a relationship you can investigate: how a recurring formal choice shapes the presentation of power in the selected work.

A useful inquiry remains open to discovery. Avoid wording that assumes a conclusion before the evidence has been examined.

items.title: TPCASTT: a poetry reading scaffold
items.summary: A second way into a poem, from literal understanding to an evidence-based interpretation.
items.body:
## When to use it
Use TPCASTT when you need a more guided first reading of a poem. It helps generate observations; your eventual argument should follow the guiding question and the poem’s particular choices.

## The seven prompts
1. **Title:** record an initial possibility suggested by the title. Treat it as a hypothesis.
2. **Paraphrase:** establish the literal meaning in your own words before interpreting symbolism.
3. **Connotation:** explore significant language, imagery, sound, and form. Explain their contributions rather than collecting device names.
4. **Attitude:** examine the speaker’s attitude and its complexity. The speaker is not automatically the poet.
5. **Shifts:** look for changes in argument, tone, perspective, or form. Test their significance through surrounding details.
6. **Title revisited:** reconsider the title in light of the whole poem. Revise your first hypothesis if needed.
7. **Theme:** formulate a claim about what the poem explores or suggests, supported by its choices.

## Turn notes into analysis
Select a revealing pattern or shift, connect precise details, and formulate a thesis that answers the guiding question. The seven prompts do not prescribe seven paragraphs.

items.title: Poetry
items.summary: Follow voice, line, stanza, sound and shifts as they shape a poem’s meaning.
items.body:
## What kind of text is this?
A poem makes meaning through language and its arrangement. It may tell a story, stage a voice, argue, ask questions or resist a neat conclusion. Its form matters, but no single feature or fixed effect defines “poetic” writing. Begin with the literal situation and the movement of the whole poem.

## What to notice
- **Voice and address:** Who seems to speak, to whom, and under what pressure? Do not automatically equate the speaker with the poet.
- **Movement and turns:** What changes from opening to ending—in claim, image, mood, perspective or relation between voices?
- **Line and stanza:** Where does a line end, and does the syntax end with it? A pause, run-on line or stanza break may shape emphasis or expectation.
- **Sound and pattern:** Repetition, rhythm, rhyme and sonic echoes can make a relationship audible. First establish the pattern; then ask what it does here.
- **Images and ambiguity:** Which concrete details support your interpretation? What detail might complicate it?

Treat these as questions, not a device checklist. A poem without regular metre or rhyme still offers choices worth analysing.

## Language for analysis
An **enjambed** line carries a grammatical unit beyond the line break; an **end-stopped** line pauses with its syntax. A **stanza** groups lines, while a **turn** is a meaningful shift in thought or direction. **Speaker** names a voice constructed in the poem, not necessarily the author's own position.

Verbs such as **qualifies**, **echoes**, **interrupts**, **recasts** and **sustains** can describe relationships between choices. Use the [analytical language bank](/resources/analytical-language) for more options, but explain the movement in the poem rather than naming devices for their own sake.

## Worked example

## Reading Up-Hill
Read Christina Rossetti's public-domain poem “Up-Hill” alongside this guide. Its repeated question-and-answer pattern joins uncertainty to reassurance. The opening asks whether the road winds “all the way”; the answer confirms the length of the journey rather than pretending it is easy. Later questions test whether shelter and rest will be available. The form gives those concerns room to recur before the final answer widens the promise from one traveller to “all who come.”

**Observation → interpretation:** the speaker asks about beds for “me and all who seek”; the reply offers beds for “all who come.” The repeated “all” and the change from seeking to coming may suggest a widening assurance, while the question preserves the traveller's uncertainty. This is one defensible reading, not a fixed meaning of repetition.

For the full close-reading sequence and an annotated paragraph, open the [Literature Paper 1 companion](/courses/literature/assessment/a718b887-02ee-4e53-acb5-808ef5214809#worked-example).

## Try it
Choose a short poem or use “Up-Hill.” First write one sentence describing what literally happens. Then trace a change between its opening and ending, quoting one detail from each. In two or three sentences, explain how a formal or verbal choice helps make that change meaningful. Finally, test whether another detail complicates your claim.

If you need prompts for a first reading, use the [TPCASTT scaffold](/resources/reading-methods/tpcastt). For the assessed task, return to [Literature Paper 1](/courses/literature/assessment/a718b887-02ee-4e53-acb5-808ef5214809).

items.title: Drama
items.summary: Read dialogue as action: follow replies, silence and stage directions, then explore a separate Bovell worked example.
items.body:
## What makes drama different?

Drama presents people speaking and acting in relation to one another. A play script is written with performance in mind: words can become voices, pauses take time, and an entrance can change who knows what. Read the dialogue and stage directions together, asking **what changes between the characters as the scene unfolds**.

A character may use speech to persuade, avoid, accuse, comfort, test or conceal. What they say matters, but so does what their speech does to someone else. A question can ask for information and demand reassurance at the same time. A reply can answer the words while avoiding the concern behind them.

Drama is not always realistic conversation. Plays can use verse, songs, choruses, direct address, fragmented scenes or deliberately unnatural repetition. Start with the conventions of the extract you have, rather than expecting every play to work like a family argument.

## Situation, audience and perspective

Establish who is present, what has just happened and what each character appears to want. Use the supplied introduction and the script. If you are reading an extract, you may not know how the conflict began or how the play ends. You can still explain what this exchange reveals and changes.

Distinguish the **listener within the scene** from the **theatre audience**. One character might accept an excuse while the audience notices a contradiction. Alternatively, spectators may share the characters’ uncertainty. Ask what information is available to each before calling a moment dramatic irony.

The playwright arranges the encounter; a character’s opinion is not automatically the playwright’s position. Avoid treating one speech as the play’s final message. Consider how another character responds and whether the scene supports, challenges or leaves that view unresolved.

In an unseen script, discuss effects on a reader or potential audience. You can infer performance possibilities, but cannot report an actor’s expression or a director’s lighting as a fact unless the supplied text specifies it.

## Dialogue as action

### Replies, questions and control

Follow exchanges rather than collecting striking speeches. Who asks the questions? Who chooses the subject, refuses to answer, interrupts or gets the final word? An unanswered question can matter as much as a long reply.

**Possible analysis:** A character who repeatedly changes the subject may avoid admitting something. A brief answer can limit another person’s attempt at conversation. Explain what is being avoided or controlled here; short replies do not always mean confidence or anger.

### Voice, register and relationships

Notice vocabulary, sentence patterns, forms of address and changes in formality. Pronouns can define a relationship: “we” may invite solidarity or presume agreement; “you” can identify responsibility or create distance. Repeated words may acquire a different meaning when another character uses them.

**Possible analysis:** A shared expression can reveal familiarity, while a correction exposes disagreement within that familiarity. Connect wording to the immediate exchange rather than assigning a fixed personality from one line.

### Subtext

**Subtext** is a meaning or pressure implied beneath the spoken words. Support it through the situation, a mismatch between speech and action, a refusal to answer, or the reply that follows. It is not permission to invent a secret motive.

**Possible analysis:** A question about money may also ask whether a partner can be trusted. Show what in the exchange makes that second concern plausible.

## Silence, stage directions and performance

Stage directions may specify movement, gesture, expression, setting, sound, lighting or delivery. They can also explain a situation to the reader that a production would need to communicate through performance. Read their wording as carefully as the dialogue.

A **pause** or **silence** gives the audience time in which no words are spoken. Its meaning depends on what comes before and after: waiting for an answer differs from refusing one. If a direction explicitly interprets a silence, acknowledge that guidance instead of treating every meaning as equally possible.

Punctuation can suggest hesitation, interruption or a change of thought. An ellipsis alone does not tell you exactly how long an actor pauses or how loudly a line is spoken. Explain the break in the sentence before proposing a performance choice.

Separate these three kinds of statement:

- **Specified:** “The stage direction places a silence after the question.”
- **Inferred:** “The unanswered question makes the possibility of rejection more immediate.”
- **Possible in performance:** “A prolonged pause could make the listener’s wait more uncomfortable.”

The third can develop an interpretation, but it should not replace analysis of the script. Do not invent tears, shouting or gestures to supply evidence the extract lacks.

## Space, objects and what can be seen

Entrances and exits change who can speak, overhear or intervene. Distance can suggest intimacy or separation; a doorway can control access. Props can become points of conflict, signs of status or reminders of someone absent. Connect the arrangement to what happens in the scene.

Distinguish an object **mentioned in speech** from one **specified on stage**. A character talking about a locked door does not establish that a visible door stands between the actors. Likewise, a recollection of sitting at a table is not necessarily a stage direction placing the present conversation there.

When the extract provides little staging, say more about the choices it does supply. You do not need a paragraph on scenery simply because the text is a play.

## Movement, conflict and dramatic form

Track the scene’s **beats**: small changes in intention, information or emotional pressure. A discussion might move from denial to questioning, then from explanation to accusation. Identify the line or action that makes each turn happen.

Long and short speeches can shape this movement. One person may explain at length while another reduces that explanation to a painful phrase. Repetition can reveal that they remain stuck, or show that a familiar word has changed meaning. A scene can end without resolving its conflict; a final reply is not automatically a conclusion accepted by everyone.

Use formal terms when they fit:

- **Monologue:** an extended speech by one character; others may be present.
- **Soliloquy:** a speech presenting a character’s thoughts, conventionally not heard by other characters.
- **Aside:** words directed to the audience or a particular listener, conventionally unheard by others on stage.
- **Dramatic irony:** a gap between what the audience knows and what a character knows.

Comedy, tragedy and other dramatic traditions can help frame a reading, but one awkward or sad exchange is not enough to classify an entire play. Explain the local effect before making a larger claim about genre.

## A practical reading method

1. **Establish the situation:** who is speaking, what has happened and what is at stake?
2. **Read in exchanges:** pair a speech with its reply. What does the second speaker accept, resist or change?
3. **Mark the turns:** where does a question, silence, admission or entrance alter the encounter?
4. **Connect speech and staging:** distinguish written directions from performance possibilities.
5. **Form an interpretation:** explain how the relationship or conflict develops, using the guiding question to choose a focus.
6. **Test the ending:** does the last exchange resolve, deepen or complicate your first reading?

Organise paragraphs around developments in meaning, not a compulsory sequence of “dialogue, stage directions, imagery.” Those choices often work together within the same moment.

## Vocabulary and further guidance

Useful terms include **dialogue, exchange, turn-taking, subtext, pause, stage direction, prop, dramatic irony** and **beat**. Terms such as **pronoun, repetition, syntax, register** and **contrast** remain useful too. Naming a dramatic feature starts an explanation; it does not finish it.

- [Literary and rhetorical reference](/resources/analysis-reference)
- [Analytical language and tone vocabulary](/resources/analytical-language)
- [Literature Paper 1](/courses/literature/assessment/a718b887-02ee-4e53-acb5-808ef5214809)

For another practice source, the [IB’s official Literature Paper 1 specimen](https://ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/dp/pdfs/english-a-literature-hl-paper-1-en.pdf) includes an extract from Alan Ayckbourn’s *Absent Friends*. Compare how extended speech and brief replies establish a relationship there. It is a specimen paper, not a past examination session; its characters and situation are separate from the Bovell example below.

## Worked example

## Read the encounter

The supplied extract from Andrew Bovell’s *Things I Know To Be True* begins after Bob discovers that his wife, Fran, has secretly saved money. The question asks how dialogue communicates **emotional tension in their relationship**. An account of the financial disagreement alone would leave that focus unanswered.

Read the whole extract before opening the analysis. The source panel offers a readable transcript and the original supplied pages. Its three reading groups are teaching aids, not divisions printed in the play. You can keep the full extract open or follow the selected exchange beside each section.

A first reading to test: **a dispute about ownership becomes a painful disagreement about what staying married means**. Fran presents savings as protection and staying as a complex choice; Bob hears evidence that the partnership was less mutual than he believed. The tension develops as they answer the same words with different understandings.

The question comes from the supplied paper. The commentary, thesis, paragraph and practice tasks are original teaching material, not an official marked response.

## Mine and ours

Fran begins with three short statements: **“It was mine. My wage. I earned it.”** The possessive and first-person pronouns claim a right to the money. Their clipped sequence leaves little space for negotiation: ownership is justified through her labour.

Bob replies by describing a bank account bearing both names. His **“There was never a mine. Just ours.”** takes up Fran’s language but replaces individual ownership with partnership. The disagreement is already about the terms of their marriage, not merely the location of savings.

Fran’s **“‘Get Out’ money”** then changes what saving means. Her mother’s experience gives her a reason to value the option of leaving: she does not want financial dependence to trap her. This is Fran’s explanation of her choice. It does not establish that her own marriage exactly repeats her mother’s.

Read the turns together. Fran defends independence, while Bob asks why he was excluded. Her account of buying and selling shares briefly stresses her competence; Bob’s short reactions return attention to what he did not know. Calling his **“Right.”** agreement would overlook the questions that follow. Its exact delivery is open, but the exchange shows that the issue remains unsettled.

## The question and the silence

Fran says she needed to know she could leave. Bob’s **“Did you… Ever need to?”** turns a hypothetical escape into a question about their actual history. The broken sentence marks difficulty in asking; it does not, by itself, specify tears or a particular tone of voice.

The direction **“Her silence is the answer.”** makes the absence of a spoken reply meaningful. Bovell does not leave us to guess whether the silence communicates: the direction explicitly says that it does. In context, it suggests that Fran has felt the need to leave. A production must make the pause carry that admission without the audience hearing the printed direction.

Bob then asks **“What stopped you?”** His next question treats the silence as an answer and presses for the reason she stayed. The sequence matters: speech, silence and another question turn a financial discovery into an emotional one.

An actor could show the difficulty through stillness, averted eyes or a change of pace. Those are possible ways of performing the moment, not actions specified in this extract. Base the analysis on the placement and wording of the silence before imagining its delivery.

## The children and the missing me

Fran’s **“The children. I stayed because of the kids.”** gives a direct answer, but not the reassurance Bob appears to seek. The two sentences repeat the same reason in different words, leaving him out.

His response, **“And me? Where was I in this picture?”**, names that omission. The short first question asks whether he mattered; the second turns their shared life into a picture in which he cannot find his place. The tension comes from the gap between an explanation Fran considers sufficient and the recognition Bob wants from it.

Fran next moves into general statements about long relationships: **“You can’t love someone for thirty years straight.”** The shift from her own experience to “you” makes her account sound like a wider truth about marriage. That can explain her experience while also making it harder for Bob to answer as an individual.

Her repeated **“the point”** gives practical survival and raising children priority over continuous romantic love. Yet she offers to stop, and Bob says he wants to know. The exchange is not simply one person speaking and the other refusing to listen. His wish for honesty helps sustain the conversation even as its answers hurt him.

## Settling and being honest

Fran’s final long speech gives staying together a basis in ordinary companionship. Repeated **“still”** connects the man at the table with the person in the bed: familiarity and continued presence become reasons to remain.

Those domestic details are images within her speech. They do not establish the actors’ present positions, a visible table or a bed on stage. Analyse what the remembered routine means before turning it into a staging claim.

The phrase **“And you settle for that.”** can suggest accepting an imperfect but enduring relationship. Bob’s **“You settled for me.”** changes its force. He replaces the general “that” with the personal “me” and turns her account into a judgement of his own worth. What Fran presents as a way of living together, he hears as being less than she wanted.

The final **“I’m being honest, Bob.”** defends her way of speaking rather than directly answering his hurt. It does not prove that she feels no love, nor does it settle the disagreement. The extract ends with honesty and reassurance pulling in different directions.

## Build an analytical response

### A possible thesis

Bovell turns a disagreement about secret savings into a conflict over what their marriage has meant. Contrasting pronouns, questions answered by silence and Bob’s reuse of Fran’s words expose a gap between her defence of independence and his need to feel chosen. Their continued conversation reveals that honesty can deepen tension as well as explain it.

### A plan organised around the relationship

- **Different ideas of partnership:** connect “mine” and “ours” with Fran’s explanation of the escape fund.
- **The cost of asking:** connect Bob’s question, the explicit silence and the answer about the children.
- **Different meanings of staying:** connect Fran’s account of ordinary companionship with Bob’s “You settled for me.”

These are possible lines of argument, not a required three-paragraph structure. Each combines dialogue, structure and the implications of specific words. Keep returning to how tension develops between the two speakers.

### Worked analytical paragraph

Bob’s reply turns Fran’s account of staying together into a painful judgement of his own value. Her repeated “still” presents familiar companionship as something that survives changes in feeling: the man she loved remains part of ordinary life. Yet her phrase “settle for that” leaves acceptance close to disappointment. Bob sharpens that possibility in “You settled for me,” replacing the general “that” with the personal “me.” His brief reply reduces her longer explanation to the fear that he was accepted as second best. Fran’s final appeal to honesty does not directly reassure him. The tension therefore comes from how one speaker receives and reshapes the other’s words, rather than from an explicit declaration that the marriage has failed.

### What makes this analysis?

The paragraph follows a speech and its reply, explains the change in wording, and connects that change to the emotional relationship. It uses the ending to qualify the claim. It does not need an invented gesture or a separate paragraph listing dramatic techniques.

For the wider process of planning and writing, return to [Literature Paper 1](/courses/literature/assessment/a718b887-02ee-4e53-acb5-808ef5214809).

## Practice and transfer

Choose Bob’s **“And me?”** and Fran’s response about thirty years of love. Write a paragraph explaining how the reply changes the terms of his question. Include a short quotation from each speaker and account for the movement from a personal question to a general statement.

Before exporting, test one claim. Replace “The short sentences show anger” with an explanation of what a particular short reply does to the preceding speech. Replace “The silence creates tension” with an account of the question it answers and the next question it makes possible.

On another drama extract, begin with its own situation. A comic misunderstanding, a public speech or a solitary voice will require different questions from this marital argument. Transfer the habit of tracing speech, response and change; do not assume every pause conceals a confession.
